candidates.text:
VENTURE CAPITAL: DEV TOOLS

The "App Builders" - Cognition, Cursor, Loveable - and others have grown at outstanding revenue pace.

But, so have oother tools not so well known that are at the AI coding infra layer. 

Our team uses Supabase and Vercel - both excellent tools... both insanely over-priced now.

All to say -- betting on coders going extinct is a terrible idea. 

These tools are designed for coders (and some also for agentic workflows).

Cognition (Devin): ARR rose from $1 MM to $73M from September 2024 to June 2025.

Many VCs passed on Devin at $1 MM.

The whole category of AI dev tools is melting faces.

The valuations of some of these names exceeds those of many well-known, strong brand public market firms (like Atlassian, Elastic, etc.)

These tools serve coders - and agents.

If you were betting on the end of coding as a profession, you're wrong.

We're seeing more code output than ever before.

We're going to see an explosion in niche, specialized coding to fill gaps that previously didn't make sense to fill.

candidates.text:
I've spent the last few posts arguing that architecture debt now has a very direct cost: agent time, context and tokens.

That's also a big part of why I built Enola.

Coding agents are very good at writing code. But before writing anything, they still need to figure out where the change belongs, what already exists, what depends on it and what they might break.

Throwing more context at that problem isn't a solution.

A codebase with clear boundaries gives an agent a smaller problem to solve. A codebase full of cycles, coupling, duplicated implementations and architectural drift gives it a larger one.

Enola analyzes that structure directly from the code.

It builds a deterministic snapshot of repositories and the relationships between them, detects architectural problems, calculates impact and gives both humans and agents a way to reason about the codebase without rediscovering everything from scratch on every loop.

It's open source, Apache 2.0, and you can run it locally:

"pip install enola-cli"

What started as a tool I needed for my own multi-repository work is now being used by other projects as infrastructure too. @cognee_ recently made Enola a core dependency, installed directly through pip.

If you're building software with coding agents, especially across a codebase that's no longer small, I'd love for you to try breaking it.

And if you find it useful, a GitHub star helps more people find it:

https://t.co/xU8sOW9c2M

candidates.text:
Interesting comments from OSTP Director Michael Kratsios on the pacing discussions. Echoing some of the prior comments from VP Vance ("if you are building Frankenstein, stop")

"Our position is if you do believe that you are developing a technology that is unsafe, that you don’t want out in the world, you can just stop it. 

You don’t need someone to force you to do that and I think thats what’s been a bit confusing about this whole narrative. 

So there’s leaders of these companies that are going out and saying we are gonna do all these measures, the government has to do all these things, when in reality they just need to slow down if they feel like they need to do so.”

Companies who are warning that their activities present an immense risk but they plan on continuing anyway should work on a better answer to this question, or should consider whether they in fact can take a greater degree of unilateral action in favor of safety and security than they have thus far.
